title: UNIT 3: STRUCTURE OF THE ATOM
notes:
✓ The atomic theory explains the nature and structure of matter.

→ Modern atomic theory describes atoms as consisting of a small dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons occupying energy levels.

title: 3.1 Atom and Atomic Theory
notes:
✓ Atom → the smallest particle of an element that retains the chemical identity of that element.

✓ Atomic theory → explains the composition and behavior of matter in terms of atoms.

→ Modern atomic theory states that atoms contain subatomic particles and that atoms of the same element have the same atomic number, although they may differ in mass because of isotopes.

title: 3.1.1 Atomic Models
notes:
✓ Atomic model → a scientific representation used to explain the structure of an atom.

◆ Major developments:
✓ Dalton → solid-sphere model.
✓ Thomson → electron embedded in positive matter.
✓ Rutherford → small dense nucleus.
✓ Bohr → electrons in fixed energy levels.
✓ Modern model → electrons occupy orbitals with probable locations.

title: 3.2 Chemical and Scientific Laws
notes:
✓ Scientific law → a statement describing a consistent natural relationship supported by repeated observations and experiments.

◆ Important chemical laws:
✓ Law of conservation of mass.
✓ Law of definite proportions.
✓ Law of multiple proportions.

→ These laws helped establish the atomic theory.

title: 3.2.1 Fundamental Laws of Chemical Reactions
notes:
✓ Law of conservation of mass → matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

✓ Law of definite proportions → a pure compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass.

✓ Law of multiple proportions → when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratios.

title: 3.3 Dalton's Atomic Theory
notes:
◆ Dalton proposed that:
✓ Matter is composed of atoms.
✓ Atoms of the same element have similar chemical properties.
✓ Atoms of different elements differ in their properties.
✓ Compounds form when atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios.
✓ Chemical reactions rearrange atoms; atoms are not created or destroyed.

→ Modern discoveries showed that atoms are divisible into subatomic particles and that isotopes of an element can have different masses.

title: 3.4 Electron
notes:
✓ Electron → a negatively charged subatomic particle.

✓ Charge → −1.
✓ Relative mass → approximately 1/1836 of a proton.

→ Electrons are found outside the nucleus and are responsible for many chemical properties and bonding behaviors.

title: 3.4.1 Cathode-Ray Tube
notes:
✓ Cathode-ray tube → a partially evacuated tube used to study cathode rays.

◆ Cathode rays:
✓ Travel from cathode toward anode.
✓ Are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
✓ Carry negative charge.
✓ Consist of electrons.

→ The discovery of cathode rays provided evidence for the electron.

title: 3.4.2 Discharge Tube
notes:
✓ Discharge tube → a tube containing gas at low pressure through which an electric current can pass.

→ It was used in experiments that led to the discovery of cathode rays, canal rays and other forms of radiation.

title: 3.4.3 Cathode and Anode
notes:
✓ Cathode → electrode from which cathode rays originate in a discharge tube.

✓ Anode → positive electrode in the discharge-tube setup that attracts electrons.

✓ In electrochemistry, electrode signs depend on the type of cell, so cathode and anode should not be identified only by their signs.

title: 3.4.4 Proton and Anode Rays
notes:
✓ Proton → a positively charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus.

✓ Charge → +1.
✓ Relative mass → approximately 1 u.

✓ Anode rays, also called canal rays → streams of positively charged particles observed in discharge tubes. Their properties depend on the gas present.

title: 3.4.5 Canal Rays and Perforated Cathode
notes:
✓ Canal rays → positively charged rays that travel toward the cathode and pass through holes in a perforated cathode.

→ They are called canal rays because they appear to pass through channels or canals in the cathode.

→ Their discovery provided evidence for positively charged particles.

title: 3.4.6 Neutron
notes:
✓ Neutron → a neutral subatomic particle found in the nucleus.

✓ Charge → 0.
✓ Relative mass → approximately 1 u.

→ Neutrons contribute to the mass of an atom and help determine which isotope of an element is present.

title: 3.4.7 Nucleus and Nuclear Model
notes:
✓ Nucleus → the tiny, dense central region of an atom containing protons and neutrons.

→ It contains almost all of the atom's mass and has an overall positive charge because of its protons.

✓ Rutherford's nuclear model → showed that most of the atom is empty space surrounding a small dense nucleus.

title: 3.4.8 Alpha Particle and Alpha Radiation
notes:
✓ Alpha particle (α) → consists of two protons and two neutrons, equivalent to a helium nucleus.

✓ Charge → +2.
✓ Relative mass → approximately 4 u.

✓ Alpha radiation → a stream of alpha particles emitted by certain unstable nuclei.

title: 3.4.9 Alpha Decay
notes:
✓ Alpha decay → radioactive decay in which an unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle.

✓ Mass number decreases by 4.
✓ Atomic number decreases by 2.

◆ Example:
²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He.

title: 3.4.10 Radioactive and Radioactive Decay
notes:
✓ Radioactive substance → contains unstable nuclei that spontaneously emit radiation.

✓ Radioactive decay → the spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus into a more stable nucleus.

◆ Common radiation types:
✓ Alpha (α).
✓ Beta (β).
✓ Gamma (γ).

title: 3.4.11 Gamma Rays and X-Rays
notes:
✓ Gamma rays (γ) → high-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from atomic nuclei. They have no mass and no electric charge.

✓ X-rays → high-energy electromagnetic radiation generally produced by interactions involving electrons rather than nuclear decay.

→ Both can penetrate matter and require appropriate shielding.

title: 3.4.12 Electric and Magnetic Fields
notes:
✓ Charged particles can be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

✓ Electric field → exerts a force on charged particles.
✓ Magnetic field → can deflect moving charged particles.

→ The deflection of cathode rays by these fields helped establish that electrons are negatively charged particles.

title: 3.4.13 Fluorescence
notes:
✓ Fluorescence → the emission of visible light by a substance after it absorbs higher-energy radiation or particles.

→ Fluorescent materials were used in early experiments involving cathode rays because the rays caused certain materials to glow.

title: 3.5 Composition of an Atom
notes:
✓ An atom consists of three main subatomic particles:
✓ Proton → +1 charge, located in nucleus.
✓ Neutron → 0 charge, located in nucleus.
✓ Electron → −1 charge, located outside nucleus.

✓ For a neutral atom:
Number of protons = Number of electrons.

title: 3.5.1 Atomic Number
notes:
✓ Atomic number (Z) → the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.

Z = number of protons

✓ For a neutral atom:
Z = number of electrons.

→ The atomic number uniquely identifies an element.

title: 3.5.2 Mass Number
notes:
✓ Mass number (A) → the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

A = protons + neutrons

✓ Therefore:
Number of neutrons = A − Z.

title: 3.5.3 Atomic Mass Unit
notes:
✓ Atomic mass unit (u) → also called the unified atomic mass unit, is defined as 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

→ It is used to express the masses of atoms and subatomic particles.

title: 3.5.4 Atomic Mass and Average Atomic Mass
notes:
✓ Atomic mass → the mass of an individual atom expressed in atomic mass units.

✓ Average atomic mass → the weighted average of the masses of the naturally occurring isotopes of an element.

Average atomic mass = Σ(isotope mass × fractional abundance).

title: 3.5.5 Isotopes
notes:
✓ Isotopes → atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

◆ They have:
✓ Same number of protons.
✓ Different numbers of neutrons.
✓ Similar chemical properties.

◆ Example → hydrogen has protium, deuterium and tritium.

title: 3.5.6 Protium, Deuterium and Tritium
notes:
◆ The three isotopes of hydrogen are:

✓ Protium (¹H):
• 1 proton.
• 0 neutrons.
• Most abundant hydrogen isotope.

✓ Deuterium (²H or D):
• 1 proton.
• 1 neutron.

✓ Tritium (³H or T):
• 1 proton.
• 2 neutrons.
• Radioactive.

title: 3.5.7 Natural Abundance
notes:
✓ Natural abundance → the percentage of each isotope naturally present in a sample of an element.

→ It is used together with isotope masses to calculate the average atomic mass.

◆ Example:
Average atomic mass = (mass₁ × abundance₁) + (mass₂ × abundance₂) + ...

title: 3.5.8 Radioisotopes
notes:
✓ Radioisotopes → isotopes with unstable nuclei that undergo radioactive decay.

◆ Uses include:
✓ Medical diagnosis and treatment.
✓ Tracing chemical and biological processes.
✓ Dating geological and archaeological materials.
✓ Industrial measurements.

title: 3.5.9 Energy Levels and Shells
notes:
✓ Electrons in an atom can occupy specific energy levels around the nucleus.

✓ Shell → a principal energy level occupied by electrons.

✓ Shells are represented by n = 1, 2, 3, 4, ...

→ Higher n generally means higher energy and greater average distance from the nucleus.

title: 3.5.10 Orbit
notes:
✓ Orbit → in the Bohr model, a fixed path or energy level in which an electron is considered to move around the nucleus.

→ Modern atomic theory uses orbitals instead of fixed electron paths.

✓ Orbital → a region of high probability of finding an electron.

title: 3.5.11 Principal Quantum Number
notes:
✓ Principal quantum number, n → identifies the main energy level or shell of an electron.

✓ n = 1 → first shell.
✓ n = 2 → second shell.
✓ n = 3 → third shell.

→ As n increases, the electron generally has greater energy and is farther from the nucleus.

title: 3.5.12 Electronic Configuration
notes:
✓ Electronic configuration → the arrangement of electrons in the energy levels and orbitals of an atom.

◆ Examples:
✓ Hydrogen → 1s¹.
✓ Carbon → 1s² 2s² 2p².
✓ Oxygen → 1s² 2s² 2p⁴.

→ Electrons occupy lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals.

title: 3.5.13 Valence Shell and Valence Electrons
notes:
✓ Valence shell → the outermost occupied electron shell of an atom.

✓ Valence electrons → electrons in the outermost shell that participate in chemical bonding and largely determine chemical reactivity.

◆ Example:
Na → 2,8,1 → 1 valence electron.

title: 3.5.14 Penultimate and Anti-Penultimate Shells
notes:
✓ Penultimate shell → the shell immediately inside the valence shell.

✓ Anti-penultimate shell → the shell immediately inside the penultimate shell.

◆ For an atom with several occupied shells:
✓ Valence shell → outermost.
✓ Penultimate shell → second from outside.
✓ Anti-penultimate shell → third from outside.

title: 3.5.15 Atomic Diagram
notes:
✓ Atomic diagram → represents the arrangement of an atom's particles or electrons.

✓ A simple shell diagram shows:
✓ Nucleus → protons and neutrons.
✓ First shell → maximum 2 electrons.
✓ Second shell → maximum 8 electrons for the basic shell model.
✓ Third shell → can contain more electrons, depending on the element.

◆ Example:
Sodium (Na) → 2,8,1.

title: UNIT 3 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ Atom → smallest particle retaining the identity of an element.

✓ Proton → +1, nucleus.
✓ Neutron → 0, nucleus.
✓ Electron → −1, outside nucleus.

✓ Atomic number (Z) = protons.
✓ Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.
✓ Neutrons = A − Z.

✓ Isotopes → same Z, different A.
✓ Atomic mass unit → 1/12 of carbon-12 mass.
✓ Average atomic mass → weighted average of isotope masses.

✓ Alpha particle → 2p + 2n; charge +2.
✓ Alpha decay → A decreases by 4; Z decreases by 2.
✓ Gamma ray → electromagnetic radiation; no charge and no mass.

✓ Valence shell → outermost occupied shell.
✓ Valence electrons → electrons in the outermost shell.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Z = protons.
✓ Neutral atom → electrons = protons.
✓ A = protons + neutrons.
✓ Neutrons = A − Z.
✓ Isotopes → same protons, different neutrons.
